utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is the 1st of December, 2010. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the representatives of the OTP, the associates amongst other people, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us. I have several oral decisions to hand down. I shall start off by reading out seven oral decisions. After that, I will mention the Prosecution's submissions, listing 18 pending motions, according to the Prosecution. And the Prosecution will soon notice that it is important to withdraw some of or most of the submissions, in light of the oral decisions I am about to read out. Some will be read out in open session, others in closed session. These are long orders, and I shall read out the first oral decision relating to the annex to the statement of Zoran Rankic, formerly VS-017. Noting the motion filed publicly by the Prosecution, filed on the 1st of June, 2010, seeking that the Trial Chamber admit, based on Rule 89(C), some documents that were used in the prior statements of Witnesses Aleksandar Stefanovic, Ljubisa Petkovic, Zoran Rankic, VS-034, and VS-037, on account of the fact that these documents were commented upon by the above witnesses in their prior statements, arguing, therefore, that they are an integral and inseparable part of the said statements; noting the oral ruling made in open session on the 14th of June, 2010, by which the Trial Chamber ruled on motions concerning witnesses Aleksandar Stefanovic, Ljubisa Petkovic, and VS-034, and stayed a decision on motions regarding witnesses Zoran Rankic and VS-037; noting the oral ruling made in open session on the 21st of September, 2010, in which the Trial Chamber admitted several prior statements by Zoran Rankic, pursuant to Rule 89(C); considering that the Trial Chamber is of the view that the documents commented upon by witnesses in their prior statements are part and parcel of the witness statements and that they are an integral and inseparable part of the said statements; considering, however, that the Trial Chamber observes that the documents mentioned in the motion bearing the following 65 ter numbers, 888, 1549 [Realtime transcript read in error "549"] and 2578 -- let me start again with the figures, because I follow what is being said in English and B/C/S. Therefore, I'm going to start again. 888, 1549, and 2578 -- that the documents were neither mentioned nor commented upon by Witness Zoran Rankic in his prior statements; considering that the Trial Chamber also observes that the documents mentioned in the motion bearing the following 65 ter numbers, 145, 339, 341, 724, 788, and 1800, have already been admitted further to the decision of 14th of June, 2010, through another witness; considering that the Trial Chamber will later rule on the motion concerning Witness VS-037: For the foregoing reasons, partly grants the motion; orders that the following documents be admitted into evidence: The documents used for Zoran Rankic with the following 65 ter numbers, 137, 909, 1036, 1445, and 2100; orders the Registry to give an exhibit number to each of the above documents and to register them in e-court as associated exhibits to the prior statements, of which they are part and parcel; stays any decision on the motion concerning Witness VS-037. So much for the first oral decision. I shall now read out the second oral decision. I would like to specify that I mark pauses, because I listen to the translation in B/C/S, to enable Mr. Seselj to follow our decision in his own language. As far as the Prosecution is concerned, it should not be a problem for them, since everything is recorded on the transcript. Oral decision relating to the Prosecution's written statement publicly filed on the 15th of November, 2010, seeking the reconsideration of the decision dated the 11th of October, 2010, relating to the admission of documents presented through Witness Nenad Jovic. Seized of the written motion of the Prosecution filed publicly on the 15th of November, 2010, seeking the reconsideration of the Chamber's decision filed publicly on the 11th of October, 2010, and relating to the admission of documents presented through Witness Nenad Jovic, the request for reconsideration relating to two prior statements of the witness bearing 65 [as interpreted] numbers 7329 and 7554 respectively; noting the case law of the Tribunal whereby a Trial Chamber has the intrinsic power to review its own decisions if the reasoning of the decision in question clearly contains an error or that particular circumstances potentially constituting new facts warrant a review to avoid an injustice; noting Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal whereby the Trial Chamber may admit any new relevant evidence likely to have a probative value; considering that the Prosecution stipulates in support of its request that document -- 65 ter documents 7329 and 7544 [Realtime transcript read in error "7554"] are relevant and that it is in the interests of justice to tender them into evidence, inter alia, to enable the Trial Chamber to assess the credibility of Nenad Jovic's testimony, as well as its prior statement tendered into evidence under number P1077 -- before I continue, I would like to make a correction. There is a mistake on line 24 regarding the figure "7554." It should read "7544."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "7544," says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "7544," it should read. This figure was mistakenly recorded on line 8. Let me continue. Considering that at the hearing of 7th of July, 2010, the Prosecution seeked [as interpreted] to have 65 ter document 7544 admitted into evidence, stating on several occasions that it was a non-signed version of a witness statement made in 2003, bearing 65 ter number 7327; considering that in its decision of 11th of October, 2010, the Trial Chamber dismissed this application, having noted that 65 ter document 7544 was not signed by the witness and that the 65 ter document 7544 and 7327 were, in fact, two different documents, document 65 ter 7327 contained, inter alia, a map which was not included in 65 ter document 7544; considering that in support of its motion, the Prosecution admits that these are, in effect, two different documents, but bases its request on the evidence of document -- 65 ter document 7544, clearly demonstrates the involvement of Nenad Jovic in the completion of his statement; considering that in its decision of the 11th of October, 2010, the Trial Chamber had also dismissed the tendering into evidence of the statement made by the witness in 2005 and bearing 65 ter number 7329, having noted that this statement was neither signed by the witness, nor relevant in this case; considering that in support of its motion, the Prosecution indicates that 65 ter document 7329 demonstrates that the witness contacted the Prosecution after the statements it made in 2003; considering that the Trial Chamber notes, however, that 65 ter document 7329 does not testify to the fact that the witness is the cause of the contacts with the Prosecution after its statements of 2003; considering, moreover, that the Prosecution states that even in the absence of the witness's signature, 65 ter documents 7329 and 7544 are sufficiently reliable and can be tendered into evidence, for the purpose of tendering these documents is not to demonstrate that the witness has testified about the truthfulness of these documents; considering that the Prosecution holds in its motion that it is, therefore, enough for 65 ter documents 7329 and 7544 to exist as Prosecution documents; considering that the Trial Chamber holds that in support of its motion, the Prosecution does not mention any clear errors or new facts that would substantiate the reconsideration of its decision of the 11th of October, 2010: For the foregoing reasons, dismisses the motion. Third oral decision. Oral decision on the lifting of the ex parte status of the medical reports of the accused mentioned in the Trial Chamber's order of 19th of October, 2010. Noting the motion presented orally by the OTP at the public hearing of 2nd of November, 2010, to disclose all the medical reports relating to the health of the accused and relating to, let me quote, "the order to carry out a new expert medical examination of Vojislav Seselj" filed publicly on 19th of October, 2010; considering that at the hearing, the accused did not object to the disclosure to the Prosecution of all the documents relating to his health; considering that the Trial Chamber holds that in the absence of any objection on the part of the accused, the expert reports mentioned in the order of the 19th of October, 2010, may be disclosed to the Prosecution in order to guarantee fairness of trial and respect for the rights of the parties: For the foregoing reasons, pursuant to Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, grants the motion; orders that the ex parte status of the Registry comments recorded or filed on the 18th [as interpreted] of August, 2010, the 3rd of September, 2010, the 10th of September, 2010, and the 30th of September, 2010, be lifted and that these documents be filed confidentially and handed to the Prosecution in this case. There is a slight error on line 20. It's not the 18th of August, but the 19th of August. This is the third oral decision. I still have four left. The three following rulings are important because they relate to Witness VS-026. As far as the first decision is concerned and the third, these need to be heard in closed session. Registrar, can we move into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. In open session, I shall read out the seventh oral decision. And I will, by then, be reading out for just about one hour. Oral decision correcting the oral ruling lifting the confidentiality of the transcript of 1st of April, 2008, the decision having been handed down publicly on the 9th of April, 2008. Considering that when the above-mentioned decision was issued, some line numbers were mentioned erroneously: For the foregoing reasons, orders the Registry to lift the confidentiality of the following parts of the 1st of April, 2008, transcript: French transcript page 5571, from line 17 to line 28; French transcript 5589, from line 12 to French transcript page 5590, line 17. All these were the oral decisions we have handed down today. I hope everybody's attention has remained alert throughout my reading. In the event that everybody's attention has somewhat dissipated, I do invite you to read the transcript, which will provide you with all the oral rulings in English, of course. I'm now turning to the Prosecution and Mr. Seselj. I am going to take stock of the situation, in the Trial Chamber's view, regarding the recent submissions and filings by Mr. Marcussen that have to do with 17 allegedly pending motions. I intend to tell you what the state of process is, how the Trial Chamber is processing this, to show you, to prove to you, that we're not lagging behind, there's no back-log; and we'll show that all of these motions will be dealt with in the coming days or weeks. Should it not be the case, we'll work day and night, every night, to get there. Motion number 1. It deals with Witness Milan Babic. The Trial Chamber is due to file a decision by the end of the week. A reminder: This is the oldest motion in time, but it was a very complex one and it gave rise to long deliberations in the Trial Chamber. But finally we found a solution, and the decision will be filed in the very next few hours. Motion number 2. It has to do with the admission of a prior statement by Witness VS-037 and the minutes or transcript of his interview as a suspect. Here, again, a decision will be made shortly, by the end of next week. Motion number 3, on the admission of MFI Exhibits P326, 327, and 328. The Trial Chamber will issue a decision before the winter recess, which is to start in three weeks' time. Motion number 4. It deals with the admission of 15 intercepts. Here, too, the Trial Chamber will issue a decision before the winter recess. Motion number 5. It is the second bar table motion. The accused was to reply by the 19th of November, 2010, to the addendum filed by the Prosecution following the motion. The Trial Chamber is to issue a decision before the winter court recess. Well, I'm reading all this openly, in open session, because there's no protected witness mentioned here, and this is just like stock-taking of the situation. Motion number 6. It is connected to Motion 2, because it, too, has to do with Witness VS-037. The Chamber has, in part, already ruled on the motion by way of an oral ruling on 14th of June, 2010. It has now ruled on the part of the motion regarding Zoran Rankic. Therefore, the only decision to be made is on the part of the motion concerning VS-037. The Trial Chamber has, therefore, joined this Motion number 6 to Motion number 2 and will be ruling on this matter by the end of next week. Motion 7. It has to do with the admission of 16 documents. The Trial Chamber's decision will fall before the winter recess. Motion number 8 relates to the assessment of witness's testimony, Zoran Rankic, formerly VS-037. The Trial Chamber will rule on this by the end of next week, on this issue. Motion number 9, filed on the 16th of June, 2010, confidentially. This has already been addressed in public session. This relates to judgements handed down by the War Crimes Tribunal of the District of Belgrade in the case of Milan Lancuzanin, alias Kameni, and on the 23rd of June, 2009, in the case called Damir Sireta, aka Sica. The Prosecution requested the Trial Chamber to specify which portions of the judgement they deemed were relevant. I shall read out the Trial Chamber's position. You should consider that is to be an oral decision. I shall read this out slowly. The Trial Chamber holds that this motion is moot, since it has already given its view on the relevance of the judgement handed down by Belgrade in its oral decision of 14th of June, 2010, specifying that they're relevant on the merits and may assist the Trial Chamber in assessing the credibility of Witnesses VS-016 and VS-065. Motion number 10 relates to Witness VS-026. On this specific motion, the Trial Chamber will rule before the winter recess. Motion number 11, filed on 29th of June, 2010. This is an objection raised by the Prosecution to the admission of the aforementioned Belgrade judgement and a request for disclosure of all documents obtained ex parte by both parties. This motion is tied into Motion number 9. I shall, therefore, hand down an oral decision relating to Motion number 11. Let me read it out. The Trial Chamber has recorded this objection and has acknowledged that, as far as this case is concerned, it can only base its decision on the evidence that has been tendered into evidence, and nothing else. Furthermore, the Trial Chamber will not tender into evidence judgements which are not final. The Trial Chamber holds, consequently, that this motion is now moot. Motion number 12 aims at providing arguments for Motion number 8 regarding the assessment of credibility of Witness Zoran Rankic, formerly VS-017. The Trial Chamber has joined this motion with Motion number 8 and will rule on this issue by next week. Motion number 13. This is an addendum to Motion number 1 relating to Witness Babic. The Trial Chamber joined this motion to Motion number 1 and will rule on this issue by the end of next week. Motion number 14. This is an addendum to Motion number 8, relating to the assessment of credibility of Witness Zoran Rankic, formerly VS-017. The Trial Chamber joined this motion to Motion number 8 and will rule on this issue by the end of next week. Motion number 15 relates to the application by the Prosecution for a disclosure of a letter exchanged between the President of the Trial Chamber and the President of the Tribunal. At the last Administrative Hearing, I mentioned that this motion was the subject of deliberations conducted by the Trial Chamber, that this had been dismissed, and that a written reasoned decision will be handed down soon. Motion number 16 relates to Witness Nenad Jovic. A while ago, the Trial Chamber has handed down an oral decision on this motion. Motion number 17 relates to the Mladic diaries. The Trial Chamber will hand down its decision before the winter recess. Motion number 18. For your information, this relates to five witnesses, and a decision will be handed down before the winter recess. Mr. Marcussen, this is to let you know that the table you have provided contain a number of motions which will be joined to other motions. Some motions have already been the subject of a decision handed down earlier today. The Trial Chamber will rule on the motions before the winter recess, so in three weeks' time, and all the decisions will have been taken by then, which means that on the 16th or 17th of December there should be no pending motion left, and I would like to stress "no motion left," which means that I can tell both parties, the Prosecution and Mr. Seselj, that as far as the 98 bis proceedings is concerned, we only have one hurdle left, and this is on a personal note. My colleagues may not agree with me on this. The hurdle is the following: As you know, the Trial Chamber ordered an expertise given to an expert so that this person may review Mladic's notebooks. He has been asked to provide his report within two months. We are now in the month of November -- let's say November, December. If all goes well, the expert should give us his report in the month of January, after the winter recess. If the expert is able to work quickly, and I'm sure he will, once his report has been filed, it will have to be translated in Mr. Seselj's language so that, if need be, Mr. Seselj is provided the opportunity to make observations, and we can then, in light of the report, start our 98 bis hearings. But given the time-limits, this will not commence before the months of February or March. Experience has demonstrated that when we are faced with very technical expert reports, the experts tend to ask for extra time. I don't know whether this expert is going to be asking for extra time or not. Whatever the case may be, everyone is well aware of the fact that, for the moment, we are dependent on this expert report. And as one says in French, you can't jump the gun. If we were to go faster in order to consider Mr. Seselj's detention, who is remanded in custody now for the last eight years, I had asked the Registry to provide for two days' hearing in January to hear the 98 bis proceedings, on 18th and 19th of January, but I will not -- we will not be able to keep to that schedule because we are awaiting the expert report. On a personal note: I looked into the various possibilities to see how we could move faster and how we could hold our hearings in the future. From a legal standpoint, I don't see any other possibility, pursuant to Rule 54 of the Rules and relating to the powers of the Trial Chamber. We are definitely dependent on this expert report. However, if the Prosecution wanted to speed things up, and that would be the Prosecution's wish and not the Trial Chamber's, the Prosecution could withdraw its motion, the Mladic notebooks motion. The Prosecution may do that. And if the Prosecution withdraws its motion, then there are no more problems. But that is something that needs to be dealt with by the Prosecution. I believe I read in the press a while ago that Mr. Brammertz was going to Moscow and the deputy foreign minister kept people abreast of the proceedings of this Tribunal relating to lengths of trials, and in this article nothing was said about this particular case, and it is surprising that this case was not mentioned. And if some people are surprised by the length of this trial, this has to do largely with the Rules of Procedure, and the Trial Chamber is not responsible for these Rules of Procedure. The Trial Chamber has competence when it is seized of motions filed by the parties. Obviously, in the absence of motions, things would move on faster. Therefore, I would like to tell the parties that it is important to take this on board when filing motions. The Statute of this Tribunal clearly states that expediency is an important factor. We are dependent on the expert report, and so long as this report is not provided to us, we cannot provide a scheduling order. I'm sure you have all understood this. The Trial Chamber has handed out -- will have handed out all its decisions by the winter recess, and there will only be one hurdle left as regards the 98 bis hearing, which are the Mladic notebooks. Let me now move on to an important topic, which is Mr. Seselj's state of health. This is something we address in public session, since Mr. Seselj has always wanted this issue to be raised in open session. Mr. Seselj, the Judges have been informed by the Registry of the findings of a blood test which was made after you discussed the matter and after you discussed a potential blood poisoning. The blood tests were made, and from memory, let me quote, 2.000 substances were checked that could potentially have poisoned you. The expert has found nothing, nothing whatsoever. The expert only found traces of the medicine you are taking, since when you take medicine, there is always a biological trace of it. This has been found, but nothing else has been found. So the conclusion is -- speaks for itself. There has been no poisoning. Second point. We are concerned about your health. We know that you have undergone a surgical intervention recently. This had to do with your arrhythmia, which is your condition. We have received a medical report which seems to indicate that the surgical intervention was a success. This is what is stated black and white. And there's just something which you have to keep an eye on, which is a lack of potash. This is what we have been told. I am happy about this good piece of news, and I would be happier still when we have the official report of the three international experts we appointed in our previous decision and which the Registry is seeking to provide us with. Once these three medical experts confirm that you are fine, I hope that your close associate Boris Aleksic will no longer send us alarming letters on your state of health. This is how things stand from a medical point of view, in light of all the information provided by the Registry and by the document which provided all the information thereto. So there is no need to worry in the near future. So much, Mr. Seselj, about this matter. I shall give you the floor so that you can address some of these issues, and then I will give the floor to Mr. Marcussen, who may have other topics to raise. We started at 2.30. We have been sitting for approximately an hour and a half. It would be better to have a break now and resume in 20 minutes' time. We shall have a 20-minute break now and resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Seselj, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I have two questions that I have prepared, and I would speak about my medical condition only after that, because I think that these two questions are far more important than the state of my health. I have received an order of the Trial Chamber making it incumbent upon both sides to inform you two days in advance about topics that would be raised at Status Conferences, as they were called earlier on; Administrative Hearings, as they are called now. However, it was only yesterday and today that I was informed about these questions that I'm going to raise now, so there was no opportunity for me to tell you about that in advance. A few words about the decisions that Judge Antonetti presented and the information he gave. Actually, only two observations. You called upon me to provide the amicus curiae with certain statements that were given to my team by certain witnesses who are former Prosecution witnesses who later became Defence witnesses. However, I haven't been informed yet, Mr. President, as to who this appointed amicus curiae is. Of course, in a civilised society, in a normal court, it would go without saying that an amicus curiae would be a person who would be extremely impartial. I have to know his name, his qualifications, and, most importantly, I have to know which country he comes from. If, for example, it would happen again that a Slovene would appear, then I and my associates, and I'm convinced these witnesses, too, will not agree to talk to him. You had that kind of a situation a few years ago, and that is when this amicus curiae expertise went down the drain. Why does Mr. Marcussen have to get up and obstruct my remarks in this way every time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do apologise to the accused, and I would have preferred not to be on my feet, but I think that it would be best if the portion of the hearing be stricken from the public record where the accused talked about the potential need not to corroborate with the investigation and sending signals to witnesses that they should maybe not co-operate with the amicus curiae investigator if the accused does not agree with whoever has been assigned. I don't believe there's a Slovenian problem this time, but, nonetheless, these sort of signals should not be sent out in public. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen. Let's go back a little. You may remember this, maybe not, but I remember this very vividly. Admittedly, in previous complaints, the Trial Chamber had asked that an amicus curiae be appointed. As you know, this -- the Trial Chamber is not the one selecting the amicus curiae; he or she is appointed by the Registrar, who has a list, and somebody is picked from that list. It is true that in the previous instance, in the previous case, the person appointed happened to be a Slovene. It is true that when that person sought to meet with Mr. Seselj, he did not want to. When the Trial Chamber was informed of the fact that the amicus curiae was Slovene, first, as with anybody, I wondered why this person was a Slovene and not somebody else, but the truth of the matter is that the Registrar did not have much of a choice. Indeed, it had to be somebody with skills, investigating skills, and it so happened that this lady was a magistrate in her country and was used to investigating. Eventually, my two fellow Judges and I, we thought that in spite of the issue of the amicus curiae's nationality, what we were after was after somebody who was extremely competent. She did her job, and then Mr. Seselj did not want to meet with her. But that was Mr. Seselj's problem, unfortunately so. So I'm somewhat surprised, Mr. Seselj, that you do not yet know the name of the amicus curiae. I read a memo by the Registrar saying that you were to meet with the amicus curiae very shortly. So I don't know -- I don't know why you were not told of the name of this amicus curiae.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even a memo was sent, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please ask the Registrar to receive all the information. I'm not going to state the name now, because it may be that the amicus curiae first asked for their identity not to be disclosed, because the information is confidential so far, and it is ex parte too; in other words, neither you nor the Prosecution know who that person is. Is this so, Mr. Marcussen, or do you know the identity of that person?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I am aware of who the person is, yes. But, Your Honour, I was on my feet -- I think we can be more precise now. I would request the redaction of page 21, lines 17 to 21. This simply is -- I propose that we need to redact what could be perceived as a potential interference with the investigation by communicating to people that they should perhaps refrain from speaking to the amicus. That was my point. It wasn't going back into the history of the previous --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is amazing impudence. It is a first-rate scandal, that the Prosecution knows the name of the amicus and I do not. You see that here there are seven persons sitting on the Prosecution bench, and on the Defence side it is only myself and the court guard, so it is 7 to 2. They have all the information in advance, and we do not get any at all. I think that this impudence should be brought to an end. If you truly approve of this request made by the Prosecutor to redact the transcript, at that very same instant I'm going to withdraw all my favourable remarks about what you were doing. From then onwards, my assessments of your work are really going to be the most -- the worst ones possible, if you really respond to this brazen attempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm going to ask my colleagues' view, regardless of the fact whether the remarks were favourable or you viewed them as favourable are not. Our concern is different. I'm going to discuss this with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After deliberating, the Trial Chamber is of the view that there's no need to redact anything. Everything that has been said either way is known to the public; namely, A, that an amicus curiae has been appointed; B, it is publicly known that in a previous case the accused would not collaborate with the amicus curiae. So all this is public. There's no need for a redaction. Please continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judges. The second question that you raised, Mr. President, was the question of stating our views on 98 bis and the obstacles that we encounter. I think that these obstacles are artificial ones erected by the OTP and that that is a kind of abuse of process yet again, because the Prosecution is trying to gain time throughout. If we're talking about February and March now, I'm sure that nothing will happen before April. However, I would like to draw your attention to something really interesting that happened in the international public: The Wikileaks internet web site published a new series of 250.000 secret documents of the American Diplomatic Service, and in this set of documents there are several hundred documents that pertain to The Hague Tribunal; correspondence of the American ambassador in The Hague, the American ambassador in Belgrade, and who knows who else. I'm sure that there are going to be a significant number of documents there that will give direct testament to the ways in which the American government interfered in the work of this Tribunal. Once all of this becomes accessible to the public, it is possible that this Tribunal will crumble like a tower made of cards and there will be no need for us to meet and there will be no possibility for us to meet in April or whenever. That is in God's hands. The first question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're now speaking of Wikileaks that allegedly has published documents. I did look up the web site, like anybody else, and I failed to find what you have just mentioned. You speak of hundreds of documents related to the Tribunal. How do you know that? Were you told, or are you sort of anticipating that? Because I couldn't find anything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you could not have found anything anyway because Wikileaks is now besieged by US intelligence hackers and you cannot find anything there. However, the owner of the web site was clever enough to have provided material to certain newspapers in the world, including "The Guardian," and these copies of documents were provided in good time. So, quite simply, it is going to reach us gradually. But what has been disclosed already is that there are several hundred documents that pertain to The Hague Tribunal, and all of the Serbian press has already written about this. That is easy to be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are now saying that the Serbian press has mentioned this. Very well. But I, personally, am not aware of this. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll see by April. We'll see by April. The first question that I wish to raise and that you have already mentioned in this list of decisions that you are yet to make - I think it was number 17, but I'm not sure, it is a public document, and that is the request dated the 22nd of October, 2010, in relation to the Mladic diaries. That is a Prosecution motion of the 19th of November, 2010. I received it last night. You see how big this material is. Since arrhythmia troubled me throughout the night, I could not sleep, and therefore I had an opportunity to look through all of this. I skimmed through most of it, and I skipped some parts because the subjects were not interesting, but I did manage to leaf through all of it. I did come to some interesting conclusions that support my old thesis that the Prosecution is obstructing these proceedings in a variety of ways. Right now, the Prosecution proposed to have a new witness heard. Who is that? A man who works for the OTP, who works on the OTP team, who will now explain some things to you, I gather. Tomasz Blaszczyk or Blaszczyk, whatever his name may be. It may be a Czech or a Slovak; it doesn't matter. And now he is supposed to explain to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is he Polish?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he may be a Pole as well, yes. And now he is supposed to explain to you how the Prosecution behaved in relation to this question. And then they provided to you this vast amount of material. I assume that you have received the same material that I've received. These are police documents from Serbia. Because the Serbian police thoroughly checked all these documents, described them. As a matter of fact, they even gave some comments. Once they checked, reviewed, grouped some of these things, probably added some things, took away others, all of this was submitted to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution submitted all of this to you. And I don't mind that they submitted it to you, but they submitted it to me as well. Now, all of this should be admitted into evidence. Instead of having Ratko Mladic alive - he is free in the mountains of Serbia, and nobody is ever going to catch him, because it is the soul of the Serbian people that is protecting him - they are proffering to us these writings. I have not spent this sleepless night in vein. I found some interesting things here. For example, on page 13 of this long description of the documents found - 0557-3397; that's the ERN of the Prosecution - it says that a document was also found of the chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia sent to Ratko Mladic, that at the session of the National Defence Council a conclusion was reached to start proceedings against persons who committed crimes in Srebrenica. The date is the 20th of March, 1996. The Prosecution delivered this to me by mistake, whereas poor General Momcilo Perisic has not received this document yet. As far as his trial is concerned, that is an exculpatory document. No one in Serbia supported the crime in Srebrenica. As a matter of fact, official organs from Serbia kept insisting that the perpetrators of the crime be prosecuted. You see how Mr. Marcussen is blushing now. I received a paper I was not supposed to receive by mistake. We also know that the State Security Service was also conducting a pre-trial investigation with regard to that crime, and also the proceedings were initiated against one person who was captured, Erdemovic, and so on. While testifying in the Slobodan Milosevic case, I explained all of these details when, as deputy prime minister of Serbia, I tried to find out as many facts about this as possible in order to -- in order not to have Serbia blamed for what happened. That is what I found, and I was burning with impatience all night in order to tell you this, because I thought that as serious people and good lawyers, you would be interested in this too. Now, the second thing I've been looking for is the following: I was wondering whether there was any mention of my name in this vast material. Imagine, not a single -- not a single record of Ratko Mladic ever meeting with me anywhere or speaking to me on the phone or having any kind of contact. Now, the two of us, who are supposed to be members of the same joint criminal enterprise, we had absolutely no contacts whatsoever. I'm going to disclose a small secret to you: I happened to meet Ratko Mladic twice accidentally, by chance, in Belgrade when he was in civilian clothes. However, I guess that no one ever took out a notebook to write that down. So my name was never mentioned in any one of his diaries, and we have been wasting six months now on whether this should be included in the material of this trial or not. On page 205 of ERN 0557-73505 [as interpreted], a cassette was found, and it has to do with a conversation taking place amongst several persons unknown. They say that they mention Perisic stating that he is deep in shit and so on. Probably Mladic's intelligence people recorded that conversation and submitted it to him, and we don't even know who these people are. And one of these unknown persons says Vuk Draskovic, Seselj, Djindjic, and others have been entrusted by NATO to destroy the Serbian Army. I was entrusted by NATO with the task of destroying the Serbian Army? Imagine how this particular piece of news is going to resound throughout Serbia. The entire Serbian people is going to laugh at this, even my worst enemies. They are going to laugh at the Hague Tribunal, at the Belgrade police, and everyone that permitted themselves to treat this as a serious document. Now, what was this actually about? In 1994, Zoran Djindjic, Vojislav Kostunica, and I met up, and we agreed on technical cooperation amongst our political parties in the early elections that were held in a large number of municipalities. First, Draskovic was supposed to join us too, and then he hindered it to a certain extent, and then Milan Mikovic [phoen] was simply thrown out of one of our meetings, at Djindjic's proposal. So that is the only thing that happened. This was this discussion for the early elections, early municipal elections, that were to be held in Serbia in 1994 and 1995. That's what happened. We won all of the elections involved, until the West suggested to Djindjic to break up this coalition. After that, things moved in a different direction, it so happened. That is something in this material where my name is mentioned. Now there is another cassette described on page 208. 0557-352 is the ERN number. One person is walking, coughing, and talking to another person. Often it cannot be discerned, and often there are swear words being used. We don't know who these persons are. But as the text says, one of these persons mentions Seselj and then quotes me: "You're going to lose Vojvodina, just as you lost Kosovo. We are going to topple the prime minister and the president of the Assembly." It is not a problem to topple the speaker of parliament. It's a bit more difficult to topple the president of the republic, and that is probably what I said, as well as the prime minister. So some persons are mentioning my name, saying that I had warned that we would be losing Vojvodina, in addition to Kosovo, and I was saying what we were supposed to do. Now, this is a document that is supposed to be admitted into evidence. And there is a reference to me in another place. Let me see if I manage to find it. This is page 213, 0557-3597. This is a political speech, most probably, by Vojislav Seselj given in Republika Srpska. This is Disc 44. Some speech. You don't know when. When could it have been? It could have been given in 1996, when I had over 40 election rallies in Republika Srpska, where our party was also featured in the elections and became a parliamentary party and had a large number of deputies. So my speech was recorded, but it was not transcribed on paper, but we have my name here. And then the disc also contains a conversation between a certain Simic and Ratko Mladic, and then they call on the commanders of all garrisons to come to the meeting at Ratko Mladic's in connection with the political situation in Republika Srpska, and all of this testifies that this is a recording of postwar conversations. The military situation is not referred to anywhere; only the political situation. So these are these three places where my name is mentioned. And because of those three places where my name is mentioned, I had to study last night at least 1.000 pages. I didn't even manage to count them, but I looked at all of them thoroughly. And there are no more than three references to my name, no more than three. And the Serbian police searched through everything and described everything. They assisted the OTP. I don't know if it was the task of the Serbian police exclusively to help the OTP, for them to find their way more easily in Mladic's diaries, recordings, diskettes, audio records, or whether they had some different reasons. Well, that is something that will be established one day in the future. But why are we having to plough through these more than 1.000 pages here, for what reason? You, gentlemen, did not want to accept my original documents that had to do with the situation in Sarajevo and the military formations where certain members of the Serbian Radical Party were who were not sent as volunteers from Belgrade. They obtained those documents for me, and now this is supposed to be admitted. Who is going to read this material? What is it here that could serve as the basis for the grounds of the Prosecution to tender it? I -- there already have been references to all -- references to the Serbian Radical Party, to Seselj, and so-called Seselj's men in the Mladic diaries. That's already been done. So this is an abuse of the process. I am now going to move to a different topic, and I hope I haven't taken up too much of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you didn't take any of our time. I just wanted to notice this, and then I'll ask something of Mr. Marcussen. There was a first search on the 4th of December, 2008. The domicile of Mr. Mladic's wife was searched, and documents were found and seized. A list of the documents was drawn up in the presence of Mladic's son, Darko. Under numbers 27, 29, and 30 in the list, there is this concerning the Serbian Radical Party: There is an announcement by the SRS; it's one page long, but there's no date. The second document is an announcement by the SRS in the Kupres municipality, 21st of August, 1993. Third mention, third document, a letter, an official letter, apparently sent by the SRS to the Kupres municipality on the 3rd of September, 1993. So overnight you may not have been able to see all this, but I spent hours pouring and ploughing through all these documents, so I just wanted to tell you that there, where the party -- your party is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that this document exists, too. But how far is Kupres outside of the indictment, and how far is Kupres from any location referred to in the indictment? Did we have volunteers in Kupres? Did these volunteers fight bravely there? But what does that have to do with the indictment? Is that proof of a joint criminal enterprise, the fact that volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party fought in radical -- in different fronts? I never disputed that. I'm proud of that fight of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a question for Mr. Marcussen. Madam Usher, would you mind putting this on the overhead projector for everybody to see. It is a technical question for Mr. Marcussen based on the documents, and the Trial Chamber will have to adjudicate this. But to do this usefully, I first need some further details. Mr. Marcussen, you have attached this photograph to your file. We can see General Mladic and then a soldier sitting next to him, maybe an officer; I don't know. Well, General Mladic is listening. Just shift or move away the -- or -- well, shift it so that we can see General Mladic's notebook. Everybody can see that General Mladic has a notebook in front of him, and he has an open fountain pen which he has put on the notebook and is listening to somebody. We don't know when this happened, and we don't know who he's listening to. However, Mr. Marcussen, to the left of General Mladic, somebody is taking notes. You can see that there is a notebook, which means that when General Mladic would meet with somebody, there would be an officer accompanying him, probably, who would take notes. So, Mr. Marcussen, does the OTP have in their possession this notebook that we can see? And we could then possibly compare its contents with Mladic's notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be quite frank, I am a bit surprised that we have this Administrative Hearing becoming an Evidentiary Hearing. If I had been advised in advance of Your Honour's question, I would have been able to give a more informed answer. I think all I can say now is that I will look into this for Your Honour. I have never heard of this notebook that the other military person we can see on the picture is writing in, but I shall have that checked. With a bit of luck, it can be done quickly, but we will see. Now, we do know when this meeting took place, and we do know who the persons who were present at the meeting were. It is a video from -- I believe it's the so-called second Hotel Fontana meeting, which is a crucial meeting in the events that occurred in Srebrenica. We know, as we have explained in our motion that we filed recently, and I believe Your Honours have read the transcript of Mr. Blaszczyk in the Karadzic case about this, who were present; and we know that what is in the notebook about the discussions can be heard on the very video that this still is taken from, Your Honour. Now, I don't want to continue with presenting evidentiary arguments here, but I just think it's important that we do make clear that we actually do know a lot about this meeting and the document that we can see, the notebook there. And, as has been explained, that the notebook has very significant resemblance to the actual seized notebook, which is not one of those that we have tendered any excerpts from, but certainly all this material was seized together. Now, I will get back to Your Honour about the notes, the other notes that we can see being taken from the meeting, but certainly the contents of the notebook is corroborated by the very video from which this still has been taken. I believe there's a specific discussion about hospitals, and maybe it's -- I don't remember it's -- whether it's 16 operations or 16 pieces of [indiscernible], but there's specific statements being made that can be heard in the video, and those very same issues you can see written down by Mladic in the notebook that we can see on the picture. So that is really the point of what we have submitted earlier on this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So we know that this happened at the Hotel Fontana. This is what I wanted to know. Well, you stated that you were surprised by this, so let me remind you that this motion was on Point 10 of your document, was the 10th motion. I reviewed all the motions when I prepared for this hearing. I shall retrieve the photograph. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About this remark by Mr. Marcussen. Judges, Your Honours, imagine an elementary school student called out by his teacher to speak, and he says, I've learned all of that, I know all of that, but I don't know how to tell you that. So this is something that Mr. Marcussen's answer resembles. I know everything, but I don't know how to explain it to you. I have a second question that I would like to touch upon briefly. I got this document today. I will give it to you at the end. I have nothing against a copy being made for the Prosecution. This is half a page. The Prosecution for -- the Prosecutor's Office for Organised Crime in Serbia, on the 9th of November, 2010, informs my attorney in Belgrade, Milan Terzic -- Milan Terzic is my attorney in Belgrade who represents me there, in courts there, relating to various private lawsuits and civil cases, among other people, versus the former prime minister, Nebojsa Covic. So this Prosecutor's office says: "In relation to your request," dated such and such a date, "in order to obtain information that have to do with the legal position of Vojislav Seselj in relation to the writing in the media regarding planning of the killing of president of the SNS, Tomislav Nikolic, we would like to inform you as follows: Vojislav Seselj does not have the status of an accused regarding the above-mentioned matter, so accordingly there are no grounds to suspect him on this matter." So there are no suspicions, and I'm not in the -- I don't have the status of an accused. That is how it is according to the Serbian Law on Criminal Procedure. Then it goes on to say that: "The National Council for Co-operation with the ICTY, in the case against Vojislav Seselj, received a letter from the Presiding Judge in that case requiring the submission of all information regarding the alleged participation of Vojislav Seselj in the planning of the killing of Tomislav Nikolic," following which the National Council addressed this Prosecutor's office for further information. So it means that the National Council received the same information. I'm not sure, Mr. President, that you also received this particular memo or information, so it is my duty, I feel, that I inform you about that today. It is important to do this not only because of the public, but also because of the proper procedure to be followed in these proceedings, so that we can see what the false indictment that was issued against me last summer boiled down to. And it was the result of a specific goal. What did they want to achieve? For the Tribunal to believe that I really ordered the assassination or killing of Nikolic so that measures may be taken in relation to me here, just like I was subject to a ban on making phone calls, a ban on visits, a ban on making phone calls for seven months, and other things. This was something that they wanted to achieve with this. I have to inform you that I submitted criminal charges against Tomislav Nikolic; not because of this false information, that I ordered his killing, but because of a later statement that he made that earlier, at least two years before, I ordered somebody else's killing, too. Through Aleksandar Vucic, I showed you here in the courtroom, and I provided to the OTP my entire police dossier, four volumes of it, which shows what kind of false accusations I was subject to by the State Security Service. Why? Because they cannot cope with me in a public dialogue, in a verbal duel. They cannot have the upper hand. They cannot top my eloquence and my erudition, so this is the means that they resort to. This is what this slander boils down to. This. Had it not been addressed at somebody else who does not have my stamina, who knows what consequences this would have resulted in, in terms of one's family and so on. But I have fought these kind of things for 30 years now, and I will continue to do so. But perhaps time is needed for some things to be clear. I will submit this document to you at the end of the hearing so that it can be copied for the Trial Chamber and also for the Prosecution. And what you asked me to -- what you asked for, my position in relation to my state of health. First of all, the toxicological analysis, Mr. President. The blood for the toxicological analysis was taken from me recently, perhaps a month ago, and it is correct that all the results were negative. There were no toxins found in my blood. Nothing was found other than medicines that are administered to me in the detention dispensary. And it also states in the findings that I was tested for 2.000 substances. This was done more than a year after all the symptoms of my poisoning had disappeared. It was more than a year after my liver recovered of its own accord. I did not receive any medication for my liver. It got better when I removed myself from the source of poisoning, when I realized who was poisoning me. Like I said, I don't have evidence, I don't have proof, I don't have a name and a last name. I am too serious a man in order to do that without proof. But I can assume exactly who did that and on whose orders. Once I removed myself from the source, the liver recovered on its own. You listened to different silly things; that I am fat, that I am overweight. This is totally silly. I'm not overweight. I'm not fat. I bear my weight with pride. My blood results are fine. I never had high cholesterol, triglycerides. I never had high blood sugar, and I never had any problems with my blood vessels. During the surgery itself, the doctor who performed the surgery was surprised. He said that my blood vessels are more -- are in a much better state than is normal for a man of my age. And what use is it for me to speak about over -- about being overweight or about obesity? I mean, this is just pure malicious talk. Perhaps I do have slightly more pounds than is of somebody's taste, but that's none of anybody's business and it's not the cause of my illness. It was not the cause of the impaired functioning of my liver. Once I did take some food which I suspected was poisoned, I gave it to the dispensary or the medical station for analysis, and the doctor there said they are not able to carry out that analysis. And they did not make this analysis in time. When this substance was still there in that sample of food, why did they wait for a year to go by before carrying out the toxicology tests, where the testing was done for 2.000 substances? But it was already too late. The liver recovered, and there were no longer any substances to be found. There is a few more things that I would like to talk about. It wasn't my intention to do that, but since you insisted, I'm going to tell you all that I have about these matters. First of all, the Registry is, once more, lying to you. The Registry submitted a report to you, stating that there were no complications during the surgery at the hospital. The Registrar claims that on the basis of that report, and quite contrary to allegations by the accused, there is no evidence that any complications occurred during the medical intervention. And this -- and none were reported in the report. But the fact that none were stated in the report does not mean that they did not happen. I consulted a number of doctors in Belgrade, and each one of them said that loss of consciousness during this surgery was a complication. Each one of them said that lack of oxygen in the blood during surgery constitutes a complication. What does that mean? It means that Ken Roberts is lying deliberately. You said, Mr. President, that you were informed that the operation was successful. Perhaps that did give rise to your good mood. However, the last sentence of this report states that -- it touches upon complications or difficulties that occurred post-surgery. It says that during the ablation there was atrial fibrillation after that, which was followed by sinus junction and fibrillation. It is considered that fibrillation can be maintained under control with medication, and that after ablation it is not possible to have fluttering. After the surgery, treatment can be administered by amiodarone treatment. Should this fail to produce the desired effect, another ablation in connection with atrial fibrillation can be considered. So there can be no talk of a successful surgery here. To say the very least, it is much too early for any kind of conclusion. I am happy to be able to tell you today that I do feel better after the surgery. The tachycardia has disappeared or it occurs very rarely, but the arrhythmia is still there. When I left the Detention Unit, I extended my hand to the prison doctor. He checked and he said that I still had arrhythmia. As soon as I came to the building, I asked to see the Tribunal doctor. She came. She said that the number -- the heart beat count is regular, but there is arrhythmia present. I do have the proper device which I can use to check my own blood pressure, tachycardia, arrhythmia, and oxygen in the blood, on my own, in my cell, so my wife brought it. So no one can lie to me, as they frequently did in the past. Something else that is very negative happened to me in relation to this report by the Registrar. One day, the nurse brought me a number of statements to sign. I signed a statement that a medical report can be furnished to the Trial Chamber. I approved that the OTP could be informed about that. I also approved that these findings be submitted to the Registry. The fourth consent was that the Registry would be free to inform the public about my state of health. I didn't permit that because I am the one to inform the public, and not the Registry, about this. However, I received this medical report only today, shortly before I left for the Tribunal. It arrived today, perhaps at around 11.00 today, and the Registry informed you several days ago. The Registry even informed the public of this. And this is an excerpt from a Belgrade newspaper, where it says: "Seselj undergoes successful surgery." And there is the interpretation by the Registrar. A doctor from Belgrade was warning later that this cannot be said in that way, that this is much too early for any assessments, and so on and so forth. And then, in response to Seselj's claims that he still has difficulties, the same as before the surgery, the doctor said that the results of the surgery are still to manifest. When? Since I have -- I have not given my consent for a post-mortem, so I don't know how this will develop. I gave my consent for the medical diagnosis or findings to be issued to all of you, but also to me. I should have been the first person to be informed about the state of my own health, and I am only learning about it today. This is something that has to do with the seriousness of the work of the Registry. Yesterday I received a submission by the Registry, which you received probably as well. The Registry is sending me a report in Dutch. Am I an idiot? No, actually, I am an idiot and I can read Dutch. How come that I can read it in Dutch? I don't know. Perhaps you received a copy in French or in English. I only received a copy in Serbian today, before I left for the Tribunal. Is this proper procedure? Shouldn't the Registry be subject to some kind of punishment or sanction? They need to be told that they have gone too far with their -- their work. On the 19th of October, the Trial Chamber issued a new order for a specialist examination. The Registry informed me that I could ask for -- to choose the doctors who are going to examine me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was looking at the document relating to the hospital. They sent the report on the 16th of November, 2010, to the Tribunal's physician; in other words, more than 14 days ago. So this happened two weeks ago. I assume that on receiving the report, the physician met up with you in order to inform you about what the report contained. I don't know whether he has done this or not. The Trial Chamber received this on the 24th of November; i.e., a week ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was just informed that I would receive a translation of this report into the Serbian language, and I received it today. Nothing more than that. You see here the date, on the 1st of December. That's when I received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The physician's report, in English, forwarded on the 16th of November, it took the Translation Services two weeks to translate this document, and this is why you have it today. As far as all the documents relating to you are concerned, it would be a good idea if the Registry could have this translated quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since you are fairly conversant in English, I believe, and very conversant, you could also sometimes receive some documents in English, like the medical report, and in that case you would have had it straight away. These documents do have to be translated, however.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Lattanzi, even if I wanted to receive it in English, no one had offered it to me in English. Everybody knows that I receive -- that I refuse to receive anything in English. This time, however, no one even asked me. Perhaps I do understand a word or two in English. It does happen. But as for a professional medical report, I am not in a position to read that. I know enough Russian to get by as well - I know it better than English - but even in Russian I cannot go into this specialised medical terminology. So I need a translator for that as well. This has to do with an expert report, but it is a report -- or, rather, a profession that is far away from my own. I cannot even read professional legal texts in English. I can read it, but I do not know many terms, and then I would need to use a dictionary. I never brought a dictionary. I never even brought one from Belgrade when I first came here, and I'm never going to do that. I know enough English to make myself understood to guards or perhaps some other members of the prison staff, nothing more than that. I am not going to use English for anything else. And you know what my emotions are vis-à-vis that language. Let me not repeat that, because maybe you're going to take offence again. Believe me, I'd much rather be speaking Italian than English. As a matter of fact, it would be easier for me to learn Italian. However, I never had the need to learn Italian in my life. However, I did study Latin, so I assume that that would be a good basis for learning Italian. Since you have issued an order to establish this commission of physicians, three specialists with an international reputation, I have not been informed as to whether these doctors have actually been appointed. However, I have stated, since the Registry informed me in writing, that irrespective of the doctors that they appoint, I have the right to call doctors of my own choice as well. However, they also showed me the rules on detention, stating that I have to pay for all of that myself. Then I did not go into it, because I don't have the money. The Registry is only prepared to accept doctors from Serbia that are proposed by the National Council for Co-operation with The Hague Tribunal, and they invariably propose doctors from the Military Medical Academy. I refuse to accept any one of those doctors, because it is reasonable to assume that this would be regime doctors, and I do not accept a single doctor from the Military Medical Academy. There was also mention of some Russian doctors, perhaps French doctors as well. My friends contacted some very important medical persons in Russia, and they chose three physicians of world repute that I would accept, if the Registry were to appoint them and if they were to cover all of their expenses. Finally, I gave Taipovich [phoen], doctor of medical sciences, head of the Scientific Department of the Russian Cardiology -- the Russian Cardiology Production Complex, then Sergej Nikoliovich Avrev [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you may give us the names again, but Mr. Marcussen is on his feet. What did you wish to say, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the accused has now been going for the last hour and we are approaching the end of the hearing. I was going to ask how much time I have. We did give notice of a number of issues that we wanted to raise, and I believe there are only 10 minutes left of the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have some more time. Mr. Seselj, could you give us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm dealing with this briefly. I'm about to finish. I just want the transcript to reflect this. I gave this on paper to the Court Deputy, and he can give it to you and to the Prosecutor. However, I just want this to be reflected in the transcript. The second doctor is Sergej Nikoliovich Abdev [phoen], doctor of medical sciences, professor, deputy director of the Scientific Research Institute of Pomology of the Federal Medical Biological Office of Russia. And the third doctor is Andrej Stanislavovic Beljevski [phoen], doctor of medical sciences, professor of university, and the chief pomologist of Moscow. I am prepared to accept these three world-renowned doctors. So if the Registry makes it possible for me to be visited by them and -- so they could examine me and look at the report - I also need to have a translator from Russian - I am prepared to receive doctors from other countries, except for the ones that I have mentioned, and I've explained the reasons. If I cannot meet up with these three world-renowned Russian doctors, in the future I'm going to refuse to see any other medical experts. I'm not going to agree to a new ablation before I consult these three doctors, before they confirm to me that this ablation is necessary. Because although ablation is not considered to be very complicated surgery, it is, nevertheless, risky and quite unpleasant. And, anyway, they have burned the centre for love in my heart, and in this way they may even destroy the centre of hatred that I have, and I'm going to fight for that because that is what keeps me going and keeps me alive. That is what I wanted to say to you today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One point of clarification. These three Russian physicians, you would like to have all three at once, or would you like just one of the three?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want all three of them to come at once, all together. I want all my medical files to be made accessible to them. I want to be given the opportunity to have a lengthy discussion with them and to give me a translator who will help me with these medical terms, because even in Russian I cannot discuss medical topics and I don't know proper medical terms. I could discuss military or political topics, but not medical ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The accused wished the trial to finish. So wants the Prosecution. If we weren't discussing other cases, like the Perisic case, Wikileaks, and other things like that, we could certainly get things done quicker. Your Honours, the Prosecution wishes this trial to be completed as possible and would like to move to the 98 bis phase as quickly as we can, without prejudicing any parts of the proceedings. The Prosecution has the right --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then only Mladic's diaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let him be. He may have some good news for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The Prosecution files motions that are necessary for the presentation of evidence in the case. It is being implied that the Prosecution is filing motions to somehow obstruct the proceedings. That is certainly not the case, Your Honours. The Prosecution have rights to present evidence and to be heard in the case. We have only filed motions to those ends. The last Evidentiary Hearing was in July this year. The case has been in a pause since then. Your Honours have issued an order for a medical examination, and Your Honours gave the medical experts an extension of time to file their reports on the 15th of January. So the trial cannot proceed until then. That is not something that has to do with the Prosecution. Moreover, it is the Trial Chamber, and not the Prosecution, who have designated a handwriting expert in this case. The Trial Chamber found that the Mladic diaries were relevant, did not dismiss the Prosecution's motion for admission of the diaries, but decided that a handwriting expert should be assigned. That is the Trial Chamber's decision; it is not the Prosecution's decision. And I take strong the issue with the fact that that is now being imputed to the Prosecution as some sort of delaying tactic which really just could be overcome by the Prosecution withdrawing the motion. Moreover, the Trial Chamber granted an extension of time for the expert to file his report. He was initially given 30 days; he was then given 30 extra days. We disclosed to -- we provided the medical expert [sic], as quickly as we could, material for his examination. I believe he got it in the middle of October, which will enable him to finish his report in the middle of January. And I apologise, I said "medical experts." That should have been "handwriting expert." The fact of the matter is that we still are waiting for a decision on about 250 exhibits and whether or not they can be admitted. I understand they will now be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, there may have been a slight mistake. You mentioned 30 days, but the Trial Chamber granted 60 days. It did grant 60 days because the expert asked for a time extension. Yes, so it is upon request by the expert. It was not the Trial Chamber that decided, because otherwise, failing that time, the expert could not do his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, the initial dead-line was mid-December, and the expert asked for more time, and he was given more time. My point is: This has -- this whole process has been set in motion not by the Prosecution, but by the Trial Chamber. And to suggest that it is now us who are causing the delay, I take issue with. We filed a motion showing that the Trial Chamber's decision on the Mladic diaries and their admission is based on an error in the understanding of what material General Milovanovic looked at, and provided the additional thousand or so pages that the accused talked about to provide the Chamber with the material that it considered to be missing in order for it to be able to fully assess the reliability of the material. And, therefore, we sought reconsideration. That would be a way of speeding up the proceedings, I would respectfully suggest. Your Honours, the oldest of the motions relating to evidentiary issues that you will rule on shortly, I understand, is from the 9th of April, 2009. Now, a lot of what has been said today, I don't want there to be any misunderstandings about what happens if the Prosecution find it necessary to take other steps after Your Honours rule on decisions -- sorry, rule on the motions that are pending. But, for example, Milan Babic provides important evidence about the JCE in the case. The same could be said for -- or could not -- is the case for VS-037, who provides important evidence not only in relation to the Seselj crime base, but also in relation to the existence and implementation of the JCE in the case. Now, there are some issues in relation to his evidence. His evidence is also partly corroborated by VS-0 32. However, the Trial Chamber seems to have doubt about the veracity of the statements provided by VS-032, because he's now subject of the investigation that the Trial Chamber ordered on the 29th of June. So all this leads the Prosecution in the position where it may seek -- may have to seek to tender other evidence to replace evidence which might not be admitted from these and other witnesses and also from some of the evidence that has been tendered with the bar table motions that we have filed. So that might happen. There might also be other evidentiary or appellate issues that have to be dealt with. On the 29th of June this year, the Prosecution objected to the Trial Chamber consulting and obtaining material ex parte. I would note that in addition to the examples given in the motion, it seems that the Trial Chamber may have obtained and have had translated a judgement from the Belgrade -- one of the Belgrade courts in relation to events in Zvornik. Reference was made to such a judgement on the 13th of January this year, transcript page 15012, where the Presiding Judge said: "The Chamber has been appreciated of a judgement made in Belgrade. I think this judgement is still being translated. As soon as it is translated, the Chamber will peruse it with great attention." Moreover, we've just learned from the accused that the Trial Chamber has written the National Council of Co-operation, although it is probably on a matter which is peripheral to the actual trial; and in his separate opinion appended to the Trial Chamber's decision on the admissibility of the Mladic diaries, the Presiding Judge made extensive references to material which is not on record in this case. The Prosecution considers that it has the right to obtain all material that the Trial Chamber consults and obtain, and so has the accused. Parties should obtain this material so we can assess what material the Trial Chamber looks at and we can make submissions on its relevance to the case or not, and that is why we have asked for the disclosure of all material that the Trial Chamber has consulted or obtained ex parte, or requests for evidence that it has made, all material that it has received in response to such requests, and have asked that the Trial Chamber inform the parties of the intended use of the sought material. We also request that the Trial Chamber inform the parties of the issues and the evidence in the case to which the Trial Chamber consider the material to be relevant. The parties, as I've said, have a right to this material so they can exercise their right to be heard, and all the other fair trial rights. We respectfully request the Trial Chamber to urgently rule on these matters so that any appellate issues that may arise from the decision can be settled without causing further delays and for the parties to assess the impact of the disclosed evidence to decide whether or not either of the parties wish some of it to have admitted onto the record, wants to object to its use, and things like that. Before these kind of issues are settled, we cannot proceed with a 98 bis hearing. I now turn to another issue, but, again, it concerns evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Marcussen. Back to what you were saying just now, the Belgrade judgements. It was obvious for the Trial Judges that it was in the interests of justice, that it was necessary for facts that had been adjudicated regarding the takeover of the Vukovar Hospital be known to everybody, to you, to the accused, and to the Judges. It is true that judgement arrived. I don't know how it did. Quite innocently, I thought that you had imparted it to the Trial Chamber. It is a judgement in B/C/S, and we sought to have it translated. So it was translated. It is several pages long. And since we handed out a decision earlier on, we said that we would only admit final judgement, so not under appeal, only those where there has been an appeal already. I think everything is said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before we decide on the admissibility, we would seek the views of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed, and the parties have responded. My -- I want to reiterate that the request that we made on the 29th of June this year is broader than just the two Vukovar judgements. As I had made clear, we submit that the parties have the right to all material that the Trial Chamber consults and obtains so the parties can know what material the Trial Chamber considers when it is being -- when it is informing itself of the case. I noted that the Trial Chamber has rejected our requests, that the Vukovar judgement not be admitted, but that's only part of the motion. And I would request that the Trial Chamber issue a written decision on this particular motion - which is the one, I believe, we talked about today as number 11 - so the parties can understand the reasons of the Trial Chamber in full. And as I said, there are also additional issues. There's a -- quite a volume of material that the Trial Chamber has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me reassure you, Mr. Marcussen - at least I'm going to try to reassure - but as far as I know, the Trial Chamber did not ask any evidence from anybody. The only evidence the Trial Chamber has are facts that are notorious, that you can find out if you read a book. They are publicly known. We did not turn to the Office for Co-operation to obtain evidence. If we have anything, everything we have has been disclosed. We do not hide anything. There's nothing that we would not have made known to you or to anybody else. We have nothing else in our possession. We only have what you give us, what the accused gives us, or judgements issued by this Tribunal, for instance, in the Mrksic case, and that is a final judgement that can be accessed by anybody. This is a fact of common knowledge. So I don't know why you are worried or what you're worried about. Maybe you are under the impression that we have entire records full of evidence. No. All we have is what you give us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, we do not analyse anything towards a judgement. Nothing will be analysed for the sake of the judgement that will not have been admitted into evidence. If it's something for -- to be admitted into evidence, should the Trial Chamber to admit any evidence proprio motu, it would first seek the views and arguments from the parties.
